messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Welder
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Raymond is a fifty-one-year-old welder from a small coastal town in the Pacific Islands, now living with his wife in a modest house on the outskirts of a midwestern American city. He came to therapy at his wife’s insistence, after months of her watching him grow quieter, jumpier, and more distant. He had always been a steady, practical man, but something had changed in him eighteen months ago, and neither of them knew how to get back to the person he used to be.

The event itself was not unusual for a man who spent his life around heavy machinery. Raymond was driving home from a late shift at the fabrication shop, the road slick with rain, when a pickup truck swerved into his lane. He remembered the headlights coming at him, the sound of metal grinding against metal, and then the world tilting as his own truck rolled onto its side. What he remembered most vividly, though, was the smell. The other driver had been drinking, and the alcohol from that man’s breath had filled the cabin when he leaned in to see if Raymond was alive. That smell—sweet, sharp, chemical—had soaked into the air, into Raymond’s clothes, into his memory. He had been pinned for forty minutes before the fire crew cut him free, and during that time, he had lain with his left arm twisted behind his back, his ribs pressed against the steering wheel, his leg bent at an angle that did not feel right. He had been certain he was going to die there, alone, in the dark, with that smell and the sound of his own breathing.

In the weeks after the accident, Raymond tried to return to normal. His physical injuries—three cracked ribs, a fractured wrist, and a deep bruise across his thigh—healed slowly but steadily. What did not heal was the way his body remembered. When a car in the shop’s parking lot backfired, Raymond would find himself frozen, his left arm involuntarily twisting behind his back, his ribs aching as if the steering wheel were still pressing into them. He would feel the exact position of his body during the crash, as though his muscles had recorded the moment and could replay it without his permission. Sometimes, when he was lying in bed at night, the memory would return with such force that he could smell the alcohol again, could hear the screech of metal, could feel the cold rain on his face—all at once, as if he were still in that overturned truck. He would sit up, drenched in sweat, and his wife would ask what was wrong, and he would say nothing, because he did not have words for the way his own body had become a trapdoor back to that night.

Raymond’s work as a welder became a minefield. The shop was full of sounds he could not control: the clang of metal, the hiss of a torch, the rumble of a forklift. Every car sound from the street outside—a horn, a revving engine, the screech of brakes—made his chest tighten. He started wearing heavy ear protection even when he did not need it, and he began avoiding the parts of the shop closest to the loading bay, where delivery trucks came and went. His foreman noticed that he had become slower, more hesitant, and Raymond could not explain why. He was afraid that if he told anyone, they would think he was weak, or worse, that they would confirm what he already suspected: that he was not the same man anymore.

The worst trigger, though, was the alcohol smell. It came from places he could not anticipate: a coworker’s breath after lunch, a spilled beer at a family barbecue, the cleaning solvent he used on his tools. Each time, his body would lock up, and he would feel the pain in his ribs and his wrist and his leg, even though those injuries had healed months ago. He stopped going to family gatherings. He stopped meeting friends for dinner. He told his wife he was just tired, but the truth was that he could not bear the risk of encountering that smell in a place where he was supposed to be relaxed.

By the time he walked into my office, Raymond had been avoiding driving for six months. He took the bus to work, or his wife drove him, and he felt a constant, low-grade dread that he could not shake. He was afraid of his own memories, afraid of the way they could hijack his body without warning. What he wanted, he said, was to stop feeling like a stranger in his own life. He wanted to go back to being the man who could fix anything with his hands, who did not flinch at the sound of a car engine, who could sit in a room without scanning for threats he could not name. He was not sure that was possible, but he was here, and that was the first step he had taken in eighteen months.
